title: Blogger Collaborations: How to Find Partners
meta_description: How to find collaboration partners and pick the right format. AI to the rescue: finding bloggers, writing a pitch, planning joint content.
og_description: How to search for collaboration partners and prepare a partnership pitch with AI.

sections.h2: Who to look for: criteria, not just audience size

blocks.text: The most common mistake is choosing a partner by follower count. A blogger with half a million in reach and moms as their target audience will do nothing for a blog about finance for IT people. An audience match matters more than size.

items: A similar or adjacent topic, but without direct competition for the same niche
A comparable audience size - a 3-5x difference still works, 20x doesn't
A similar delivery style: if you're serious and your partner only jokes, the audiences won't line up on expectations
An active, not dead audience - look at the comments, not just the follower count

blocks.text: AI helps here at the analysis stage: load a description of your audience and ask it to sketch out a list of topics and blog formats worth looking for overlap with. After that, you check specific people by hand.
Manual searching through feed recommendations works, but it's slow. A few tricks speed the process up.
Look at who actively comments on posts by bloggers in your niche - these are often the future mid-sized partners who aren't yet spoiled by collaboration offers.

Ask the AI to put together a list of search query formats: blogger roundups by niche, hashtags, topical directories. It won't hand you ready-made names, but it will narrow the search area many times over.

rows: The interest match is already there

blocks.text: A joint format should solve a problem for both sides, not just be an excuse to tag each other. Here are the formats that most often reach a result rather than staying a one-off activity.

items: A mutual interview - you're a guest on your partner's channel and vice versa, in a Q&A format
A joint checklist or guide that each of you publishes on your own channel
A week-long marathon or challenge with a shared hashtag
Breaking down one topic from two different points of view

blocks.text: The best collaboration looks like a natural continuation of both sides' content, not like advertising each other in a single go.

sections.h2: How to write a pitch that gets a reply

blocks.text: A short, impersonal message like "hi, let's do a collab" almost always gets ignored. Specifics work: exactly what you're proposing, why this particular person, and what they get out of it.

Here AI saves time on the draft: describe your idea, your audience and the partner's platform, and you'll get a structured pitch. Then add personal details - what you like about their content, why you chose them specifically - and send it.
Even a well-chosen partner won't save a collaboration if you skip the organizational details.

items: No clear publishing date for both sides - the material comes out out of sync
Not discussing in advance who publishes what and in which format
Forgetting to agree on mentions and links to each other
One side prepares while the other drags things out until the last day

faq.q: Where do I start looking for a collaboration partner?
faq.a: By defining your audience: who else your content would be useful to besides your current followers. Then look for bloggers with exactly that audience, not with the largest follower count.

faq.q: Can AI find specific bloggers for a collaboration on its own?
faq.a: It can suggest topics, formats and search queries, but the specific real people and how current they are right now need to be checked by hand.

faq.q: How do I tell that a collaboration won't work?
faq.a: If the audiences overlap by less than 20-30% in interests or delivery style, the result is usually weak - followers don't click through and don't stay.

faq.q: Is it worth collaborating with a blogger 10 times bigger?
faq.a: You can, but don't expect an equal exchange. Usually in such a pairing the big partner gives reach and the small one gives a fresh format or narrow expertise.

faq.q: How often should I do collaborations so it doesn't look like spam?
faq.a: Once every month or six weeks is plenty. Do it more often and the audience starts to see it as an ad conveyor belt rather than a genuine partnership.
